title: The Assassination of Martin Luther King, Jr. Part II
summary: Part two of the Stuff You Should Know two-parter on the assassination of Martin Luther King Jr. Covers the FBI manhunt and investigation, the murder weapon traced to Aeromarine Supply in Birmingham, James Earl Ray's fingerprints and aliases, his flight via Toronto, Lisbon, and London, and his capture at London's Heathrow-bound passport check. Discusses his petty criminal background, his 1969 guilty plea and recantation, his prison escape and death in 1998, and the conspiracy theories: the "Raoul" claim, the St. Louis bounty theory from the 1978 House Select Committee, the 1990s HBO mock trial, Lloyd Jowers's claims, the 1999 civil wrongful-death verdict, and the Justice Department's 2000 dismissal of Donald Wilson's claims. Closes with the counterfactual of King's legacy, Johnson's civil rights legislation, the push for the federal holiday (first observed 1986; Arizona holdout), and listener mail correcting a math explanation.

segments.title: Opening of part two
segments.summary: Josh introduces part two of the MLK assassination two-parter, picking up with the investigation and manhunt.
topics: Stuff You Should Know part two

segments.title: Murder weapon and manhunt begins
segments.summary: The FBI traces the rifle's serial number to Aeromarine Supply in Birmingham, Alabama, where a man using the alias Harvey Lomyer bought it days before the killing. Prints match James Earl Ray, who escaped a Missouri prison in 1967. Witnesses at Bessie Brewer's boarding house identify him, and the FBI issues an arrest indictment on May 7 and an international wanted poster.

segments.title: Ray's aliases and flight abroad
segments.summary: Ray used many aliases in the year after the shooting, including supporting George Wallace's campaign, dance and bartending classes, and a failed porn venture in Mexico. He fled to Toronto, obtained a Canadian passport under the name Raymond George Sneyd, then in Lisbon got a corrected passport with the spelling changed to Snead, and went to London and asked a Daily Mail reporter, Ian Colvin, about mercenaries before heading to Brussels.

segments.title: Arrest in London
segments.summary: Ray was caught at London's passport check when a checker noticed he carried two Canadian passports. A police officer took him into custody; he was carrying a thirty-eight pistol.

segments.title: Extradition, guilty plea, and recantation
segments.summary: Ray was flown back to the US on July 19 and pleaded guilty, avoiding a trial, on the advice of attorney Percy Foreman, who feared a death sentence. He received 99 years, a two-hour hearing with no evidence presented. Three days later he recanted, tried for a new trial, and escaped in 1977 before being recaptured. He died in prison in 1998.

segments.title: James Earl Ray's criminal background
segments.summary: Ray grew up impoverished in Missouri, dropped out of high school at sixteen, was discharged from the army in 1948 for ineptness, and was a petty criminal in and out of jail. He was serving a twenty-year robbery sentence when he escaped in 1967. Hosts describe his bungled crimes, including bungled robberies in London after the assassination.

segments.title: Questions about a conspiracy
segments.summary: The hosts say the idea that Ray acted alone is hard to accept given how he funded a year on the run and fled abroad. They mention the 'Raoul' figure Ray claimed set him up, whose description changed, and the 1978 House Select Committee on Assassinations, which found a likely conspiracy and pointed to two St. Louis men, John R. Kaufman and John H. Sutherland, who supposedly put a bounty on King.

segments.title: Coretta Scott King and Dexter King visit Ray
segments.summary: Coretta Scott King suspected the FBI. Dexter King visited Ray in prison, asked if he killed his father, and came away believing Ray was set up. Biographer David Garrow called Dexter King's support embarrassing.

segments.title: 1990s conspiracy revival: HBO mock trial, Lloyd Jowers, civil trial
segments.summary: William Pepper, Ray's later attorney, produced an HBO mock trial in which the mock jury acquitted Ray. Lloyd Jowers, who owned Jim's Grill beneath Bessie Brewer's boarding house, then claimed a conspiracy involving Memphis police, the FBI, and the mafia, and said he was paid to arrange the killing. The King family won a civil wrongful-death verdict against Jowers and others, and the Justice Department investigated Donald Wilson's claims about JFK papers found in the Mustang, concluding in 2000 they were unfounded. Biographers Percy Foreman and William Bradford Hughey believed Ray acted alone. Investigative reporter George Mills reported Ray smuggled money out of prison.

segments.title: What if King had lived
segments.summary: Hosts discuss King's rapid martyrdom and polling shifts, citing a 1966 poll and a 2011 poll, and a 1968 survey of college trustees whose views shifted after the assassination. They discuss Lyndon Johnson using the moment to pass the Fair Housing Act, King's opposition to Vietnam and the rift with Johnson, possible LGBTQ advocacy alongside Bayard Rustin, and King's unlikely presidential run, including an offer to join a People's Party ticket with Benjamin Spock.

segments.title: Martin Luther King Jr. Day and Arizona
segments.summary: The campaign for a federal holiday began days after King's death. Representative John Conyers introduced the bill each year until President Reagan signed it in 1983; first observed in 1986. Arizona was the last holdout until the NFL's 1993 Super Bowl threat changed its position.

segments.title: Listener mail: trilateration correction
segments.summary: Listener Andrew White, an electrical engineer in Knoxville, Tennessee, corrects Josh's explanation of drawing distance circles from a city, noting the compass should be set to the radius, not the diameter.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Closing reminder that the show is produced by iHeartRadio and listener email address is given.
